newsitem.title: INDIA: India increases defence budget, but worries remain.
newsitem.headline: India increases defence budget, but worries remain.

text.p: India gave its defence budget a shot in the arm with a rare 23 percent rise on Friday, but analysts said the money was still not enough to fund the military's growing shopping list.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram allocated 356.20 billion rupees ($9.9 billion) in the annual budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) against 294.98 billion the previous year.
Chidambaram also promised to provide additional funds for the military's capital expenditure, if needed, later this year.
"I am happy with the budget," Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav told Reuters. "The finance minister has promised unlimited support for defence. What more can one ask for?"

But defence analyst Brahma Chellaney said much of the newly budgeted funds would be mopped up by a proposed increase in salaries for the nation's 1.14 million strong defence forces, among the world's largest.
"The army has a long shopping list," Chellaney said. "Where will they get the money from?"
Former army general Ashok Mehta agreed the defence budget was inadequate to meet all the defence requirements.
"There's hardly any money in this for all the tasks ahead," he told Reuters.

Analysts have said New Delhi might be tempted to consider going nuclear to beef up its defences in the short term to stem the erosion in the defence budget, estimated last year to be 2.26 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).

"In the 1980s it used to be around three percent of GDP but since 1987 the budget has hovered a little above two percent," Jasjit Singh, director of the state-funded Institute of Defence Studies and Analyses, told Reuters earlier this week.
The proposed 1997/98 defence budget would amount to about 2.4 percent of the year's projected GDP.

"Everyone knows, and no one better than the army, that the money has not been coming forth to modernise ageing weaponry," Jasjit Singh said. "The navy recently retired an aircraft carrier and will lose another one in three or four years. The navy badly needs new submarines too."
He said the Indian Air Force was losing an average of 24 aircraft annually in crashes, and needed a complement of at least 350 combat planes in the next 10 years.
According to Defence Ministry sources India now has 22 squadrons of some 440 ground attack aircraft and 20 squadrons of 375 interceptor fighter planes.
The army was coping with old Soviet-supplied tanks and needed new 155-mm field guns.
"This budget falls way short of the nation's need to beef up the defence," former finance minister Jaswant Singh said.

Jaswant Singh's rightwing Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) is regarded as hawkish on India's defence preparedness and advocates the development of nuclear weapons, which New Delhi says it can build but does not want to for now.
India, which exploded a nuclear device in 1974, says its nuclear programme is peaceful.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's United Front coalition is often criticised by defence ministry officials who say the government was more interested in doling out populist subsidies than looking after the defence forces. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
